passages.title: Oaths on sacred lands and humanity's best form
passages.tafsir:
Allah swears by the fig and the olive, by Mount Sinai, and by the city of security — and the thing He swears to is not a place at all, but *you*: that the human being was made in the best form there is. Ayat 1–3 are the oath; ayah 4 is what the oath is sworn about; ayat 5–6 tell us what becomes of that magnificent creature, and who escapes the fall.

## The three places, and why these three

Ibn Kathir records that the early scholars differed over whether "the fig" and "the olive" mean the fruits themselves or sacred places.

- **Al-'Awfi reports from Ibn 'Abbas** that *at-tīn* means the Masjid of Nuh built upon Mount Al-Judi.
- **Mujahid** said simply, "It is this fig that you have" — the fruit itself.
- On *az-zaytūn*, **Ka'b Al-Ahbar, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd and others** said it is the Masjid of Jerusalem (Bayt Al-Maqdis); **Mujahid and 'Ikrimah** said it is "this olive which you press" for oil.
- On **Tur Sinin** (ayah 2), Ka'b Al-Ahbar and several others said it is the mountain upon which Allah spoke to Musa.
- On **"this city of security"** (ayah 3), Ibn Kathir reports Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Al-Hasan, Ibrahim An-Nakha'i, Ibn Zayd and Ka'b Al-Ahbar all saying it means Makkah — and adds, "There is no difference of opinion about this."

Ibn Kathir then relays what some of the Imams drew out of the sequence: these are **three different places, and to each of them Allah sent a Messenger from among the Leading Messengers, who delivered the Great Codes of Law.** The land of the fig and the olive is Jerusalem, where Allah sent 'Isa bin Maryam. Mount Sinin is Mount Sinai, where Allah spoke to Musa bin 'Imran. And the third is Makkah — the city of security where whoever enters is safe, and the city in which Muhammad ﷺ was sent.

They said these three places are mentioned at the end of the Tawrah: Allah "has come from Mount Sinai" — the one upon which He spoke to Musa; "and shined from Sa'ir" — the mountain of Jerusalem, from which He sent 'Isa; "and appeared from the mountains of Faran" — the mountains of Makkah, from which He sent Muhammad ﷺ. Ibn Kathir notes two things about the ordering. They are mentioned **according to their order of existence in time**; and the oath climbs — Allah "swore by a noble place, then by a nobler place, and then by a place that is the nobler than both of them."

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** reads the oath as taken by four objects: two trees (the fig tree and the olive tree), then Tur, the mount of Sinai, then the City of Makkah. The two trees are specified because they possess abundant blessings and advantages in the same way as Tur and the City of Makkah possess abundant blessings. And some authorities, it says, hold that the fig and the olive symbolise here **the lands in which these trees predominate** — the countries bordering on the eastern part of the Mediterranean, especially Palestine and Syria. Most of the Prophets, peace be upon them, lived and preached in these lands, Ibrahim among them, and Ibrahim was made to migrate from there to Makkah. Read that way, the oaths comprehend **all the holy places where Allah-inspired men were born and raised as Prophets**: Syria as the land and home of the Prophets, Mount Sinai stressing specifically the messengership of Musa where Allah spoke to him, and the "Peaceful City" as the birthplace and residence of the Final Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

So the sworn testimony is the whole geography of revelation itself — every soil on which guidance came down. And what does that chorus of sacred ground testify to?

## Ayah 4: "the best form"

Ibn Kathir marks ayah 4 plainly: **this is the subject being sworn about.** Allah created man "in the best image and form, standing upright with straight limbs that He beautified."

The key word is **taqwīm**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives its literal sense: *to set a thing aright, or lay the foundation straight or even; or to form something into an appropriate shape in a moderate regulation.* It is not a word about decoration; it is a word about **being correctly and evenly built**. So the ayah signifies that man has been endowed with the best natural powers and qualities which other creatures have not been endowed with — and physically too he is cast in the best composition, having no parallel among creatures.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Ibn 'Arabi's assertion that there is no creature of Allah more beautiful than man, because besides granting him life Allah gave him knowledge, power, speech, hearing, sight, planning and wisdom; "All these, in fact, are the qualities of Allah," as that passage puts it. It then brings a hadith it attributes to **Bukhari and Muslim**: *"Allah has created Adam in His image."* And it immediately gives **Qurtubi's** reading of it: it could only mean that man has been characterised by *some of the qualities of Allah*, **because Allah is beyond any physical shape or image**.

Read Qurtubi's clause carefully, because it is doing the protective work here. Whatever is being said about knowledge, speech, hearing and sight in man, the one thing this hadith cannot be taken to mean — on the explanation Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is relaying — is that Allah has a shape or an image. Man is a creature who has been given something; Allah is not thereby made like His creation.

**The judge who saved a marriage.** Qurtubi, as related in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, cites a story that puts this ayah to work. 'Isa Ibn Musa Hashimi was a high-ranking officer in the royal court of Caliph Abu Ja'far Mansur, and he loved his wife very much. Sitting with her one moonlit night he suddenly cried out: "You are divorced thrice if you are not more beautiful than the moon." As soon as she heard it she went into seclusion and veiled herself, on the grounds that a threefold express divorce had been pronounced on her. He had said it in jest — but the law of express divorce is that it becomes effective whether uttered jokingly or seriously. He spent the night restlessly and in grief, and the next morning laid the whole matter before the Caliph, who invited all the jurists of the city and put the case before them. They agreed unanimously that the divorce had become effective, because no human being could possibly be more beautiful than the moon. One scholar stayed silent — a student of Imam Abu Hanifah. Asked why he was so quiet, he recited "Bismillah to the end," then recited Surah At-Tin, and explained: "Ruler of the Faithful, Allah says that He has created man in the best composition, in the finest mould. Nothing can be more beautiful than man." Hearing this, the assembled scholars and jurists were perplexed; none of them opposed him, and Mansur ordered that the divorce was not effective.

The story is told to establish a point, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān spells it out: man is the most beautiful creation of Allah **outwardly and inwardly** — in elegance and attractiveness, and in bodily structure. Every limb moves in many different ways. The thumb alone is a masterpiece of creation without which man could not hold things. The ears, eyes, mouth, teeth, nose, chest and stomach are each wonders in their own right, and gathered together on the head they form a beautiful and coherent assortment, each one complementing the other. The flexibility of the tongue, the arrangement of the teeth and the mastery of the vocal cords let the same throat roar like a lion and sing as beautifully as a nightingale. All of it makes the human body look like a sophisticated factory where automatic machines accomplish delicate work — which is why philosophers call man a *microcosm*, a miniature universe that epitomises the large one.

## Ayah 5: the fall — two readings

"Then We reduced him to the lowest of the low." The word **thumma** ("then") is the hinge of the surah: the same creature made in the best form is brought down. But down to what?

**First view — the Hellfire.** Ibn Kathir reports this from Mujahid, Abu Al-'Aliyah, Al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and others: after this attractiveness and beauty, the destination is the Hellfire **if they disobey Allah and belie the Messengers**. Ibn Kathir points out that this is why the next ayah follows — "Save those who believe and do righteous deeds" — and that it parallels Sūrat al-'Asr: "By Al-'Asr. Verily man is in loss, except those who believe and perform righteous deeds" (103:1–3).

**Second view — decrepit old age.** This has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah, and Ibn Kathir notes that **Ibn Jarir preferred this explanation**. 'Ikrimah even said, "Whoever gathers the Qur'an — that is, memorises it all — then he will not be returned to decrepit old age." Ibn Kathir's objection is exegetical rather than dismissive: even if that were the meaning, it would not be correct to exclude the believers from it, because some of them too are overcome by the senility of old age. So he settles on the first view.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān develops the second reading with real feeling, on the authority of **Dahhak and others as cited by Qurtubi**. In the prime of his life a man brims with strength and vigour and all his faculties function at their best; as he ages he grows physically weaker, his health deteriorates all the time, he even begins to lose his good looks, and he becomes useless and a burden to others. Other animals, by contrast, stay useful to the end of their lives — milk, mounting, carrying loads — and even when they are slaughtered or dead their hide, hair and bones are still put to use. Man, when he falls ill or grows old, is unable to do anything from a worldly point of view, and when he dies no part of his body benefits any man or animal. "The lowest of the low," on this reading, refers to **bodily condition**: the body bent over, the legs barely carrying him, the man who once supported others now needing others to support him.

**A third framing** is noted in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān from *al-Mazhari*: some commentators say that "We turned him into the lowest of the low" does not refer to human beings in general at all, but specifically to the unbelievers, who destroyed the best composition Allah gave them, human perfection, honour and intellect by pursuing physical pleasures — and as a result of that ingratitude are turned into the lowest of the low. On this reading the exception in ayah 6 carries its most basic sense: the believers are simply not turned into the lowest of the low.

## Ayah 6: the reward that never runs out

"Except those who believe and do good — they will have a never-ending reward." Ibn Kathir glosses *ghayr mamnūn* directly: **a reward that will not end.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to head off a misreading. The exception does not mean that believers will not attain to decrepit old age — some of them too are overcome by its senility. What it means is that **they do not suffer a big harm from it**. Those who suffer are the ones who spent their entire energy on improving a physical condition that has now ended, and who have no portion of it waiting in the Hereafter. The believer, even in decrepitude, never becomes useless: he can still accumulate rewards — comfort and high positions — for a Hereafter that is eternal.

And what of the stretch when he is too frail to act? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that during the period of senility, when he is unable to do righteous deeds, the good deeds he used to do in good health are recorded in his Record Book. It relates from **Sayyidna Anas** that the Prophet ﷺ said that when a Muslim falls ill, Allah instructs the recording angels to record the good deeds he used to perform in good health. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that al-Baghawi transmitted it in *Sharh-us-Sunnah* from Abu Musa, and that **Bukhari** has reported the same rewards for a traveller and for a person suffering from a disease.) The ledger keeps filling while the hands lie still.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers one more thought on why the verse says "a reward never ending" rather than naming the rewards and blessings of Paradise: it could signify that the reward **starts in this mortal world** and continues in the Hereafter eternally — Allah gathers around such people in their decrepit old age sincere companions who benefit from them spiritually until the last moment of their life and serve them in every possible way. The righteous servants of Allah in decrepitude are productive, at exactly the point where the senile and the unwell are generally thought to be unproductive.

## Living it

Take the passage as one movement. Allah swears by the very grounds where He sent Musa, 'Isa and Muhammad ﷺ — and swears to your worth, not to their glory. You were built upright, with straight limbs that He beautified, endowed with the best natural powers and qualities no other creature was given. Then comes *thumma*: that gift can be squandered until its owner ends at the bottom — whether one reads that as the Hellfire, as the ruin of old age, or as the disbeliever's self-inflicted collapse. The only exit named is the one in ayah 6 — **belief plus righteous action** — and its payoff is the single thing that does not end.

There is a quiet footnote from the Sunnah about how the Prophet ﷺ carried these words. Ibn Kathir opens with Malik and Shu'bah narrating from 'Adi bin Thabit, from **Al-Bara' bin 'Azib**, who said that the Prophet ﷺ used to recite *"At-Tin waz-Zaytun"* in one of his rak'ahs while travelling — "and I have never heard anyone with a nicer voice or recitation than him." Ibn Kathir notes that the Group has recorded this hadith in their books. A surah about the human being at his finest, recited on the road, in the most beautiful voice its hearers ever knew.

passages.title: Rhetorical rebuke: denying the Judgment
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah At-Tīn 95:7–8 — "So what, after all this, makes you deny the Judgment?"

These two closing ayat turn the whole sūrah on the listener. Everything before them has been building a case, and now Allah stops describing and starts asking. Ayah 7 puts a question to the human being; ayah 8 closes with a second question that carries the sūrah's warning and its comfort at once: **is Allah not the best of judges?**

## "After this" — what the question rests on

The force of ayah 7 sits in one small phrase: *baʿdu* — "after this," "after all this."

Ibn Kathir reads the question this way: *"in the recompense that will take place in the Hereafter. For indeed you know the beginning, and you know that He Who is able to begin (the creation) is also able to repeat it which is easier. So what is it that makes you deny the final return in the Hereafter after you have known this?"*

So "after this" reaches back over what the sūrah has already laid out. Ayah 4 declared the subject Allah swore about: **"Verily, We created man in the best form"** — which Ibn Kathir explains as man created *"in the best image and form, standing upright with straight limbs that He beautified."* Ayah 5 said He then reduced him to *the lowest of the low.* Ayah 6 excepted those who believe and do righteous deeds, for whom there is *a reward without end* — Ibn Kathir glosses that simply: a reward *"that will not end."*

On ayah 5 the commentators differed, and it is worth knowing only in passing here. Ibn Kathir reports that Mujāhid, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Zayd and others understood *the lowest of the low* as the Hellfire, while the meaning of decrepit old age was reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿIkrimah and preferred by Ibn Jarīr; Ibn Kathir himself settles on the first. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, for its part, speaks of "the revolution that He brought about in his old age." Either way, the ground under ayah 7 is the same.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers that ground into a sentence: *"In the preceding verses man is made to realise that Allah created him, He bestowed on him special favours and the revolution that He brought about in his old age. Man will move from stage to stage, finally reaching the grave and the Hereafter."*

That is the "this." A man who has seen himself made, shaped, and then carried through stages he never chose has already been shown the argument. Ayah 7 does not introduce new evidence. It asks why the evidence already in his hands has not moved him.

## "What makes you deny?" — the question has an addressee

Ibn Kathir stops at the words **fa-mā yukadhdhibuka** — *Then what causes you to deny* — and does not leave the question floating in the abstract. He names who is being asked: **"O Son of Adam!"**

And what is being denied is named too. Ibn Kathir glosses *bi-l-dīn* as *"the Recompense"* — *"the recompense that will take place in the Hereafter."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same word "the Requital." This is the day of settling accounts.

Notice also the tone of ayah 7. Maʿārif captures it exactly: *"He has seen the scenes of Divine omnipotence and revolutions - how dare he denies and rejects the Hereafter!"* It is astonishment, not curiosity.

**The logic underneath is simple and devastating.** Ibn Kathir spells it out: you know how you began. You know that the One able to begin a thing is able to repeat it — and repeating is easier. On that reading, denial of the Hereafter is not a conclusion drawn from evidence; it comes *after* the evidence, in spite of it. The passage is not asking the denier for his argument so much as showing that he is denying something he has already been shown.

## Ayah 8: "Is not Allah the best of judges?"

**اَلَيْسَ اللّٰهُ بِاَحْكَمِ الْحٰكِمِيْنَ**

Ibn Kathir's rendering is *"Is not Allah the best of judges?"*, and he explains it: *"is He not the best of judges, Who does not oppress or do any injustice to anyone?"* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same phrase *"Is Allah not the Greatest Ruler of all the rulers?"* The two renderings stand side by side in the commentaries.

Then Ibn Kathir draws out the consequence, and it is the sūrah's final turn: *"And from His justice is that He will establish the Judgement, and He will give retribution to the person who was wronged in this life against whoever wronged him."*

Read that alongside ayah 7 and the passage settles into place. Ibn Kathir does not leave Allah's justice as an abstract quality to be admired; he ties it directly to the Judgement itself and to the repayment of the one who was wronged. The question of ayah 8 is therefore not decoration at the end of a sūrah. It is where ayah 7's rebuke was pointing all along.

## The answer we are taught to give

Because ayah 8 is a question, there is an answer to it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that **Sayyidnā Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him)** narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said that while reciting Sūrah At-Tīn, when one reaches its end — *"Is Allah not the Greatest Ruler of all the rulers?"* — one should recite:

> **بلٰی وَاَنَا عَلٰی ذٰلِکَ مِنَ الشّاھِدِینَ**
> *"Yes, indeed, Allah is the Ruler of the rulers, and I bear witness to it."*

A word of honesty about the sourcing: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays this narration without naming a hadith collection and without giving a chain of transmission. So the teaching is conveyed here as Maʿārif reports it, and no collection is claimed for it. Maʿārif adds that the jurists have ruled it **mustaḥabb** — preferable and desirable, though not obligatory — to recite these words.

Look at what that little response does. Ayah 8 asks whether Allah is not the most just of judges, and the servant does not merely agree — he enrols himself as a **witness**. The sūrah that opened with Allah's oaths closes with the servant giving testimony back.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's commentary on Sūrah At-Tīn ends at exactly this point.

## Living it

**Stop trying to answer ayah 7 cleverly.** On Ibn Kathir's reading the question is not an invitation to debate. If a stubbornness about the Hereafter ever stirs in you, the honest response is not to reason harder but to admit — as he puts it — that you already *know the beginning*, and that the One who began you is able to repeat it, which is easier.

**Let ayah 8 be your consolation when you are wronged.** Ibn Kathir's words are precise: part of Allah's justice is that He will *"give retribution to the person who was wronged in this life against whoever wronged him."* Injustice you cannot undo is not injustice that goes unrecorded. The Judge who *"does not oppress or do any injustice to anyone"* has not forgotten your case.

**And let it be your restraint when you are the one with power.** The same Judgement that repays the wronged is the Judgement that will be established over everyone.

**Say the words.** Next time you recite Sūrah At-Tīn and reach *"Is Allah not the Greatest Ruler of all the rulers?"*, answer it: *balā wa anā ʿalā dhālika min al-shāhidīn.* Yes, indeed — and I bear witness to it. The Qur'an asked you a question. It is a fine thing to be counted among those who reply.
